name: Chloe Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't connected to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and what you say stays confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's a small place, just three of us in the back of an old printer's on Church Lane. Dennis owns it, he's sixty-three, and we do whatever the town needs: the parish newsletter, order-of-service booklets for funerals, kit badges for the football club, logos for the farm shop. I'm still learning, Dennis checks everything I do, and I don't mind that, he knows the trade.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the part you care about most?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The funeral booklets, strangely. Families come in grieving, with a shoebox of photos, and you make something they keep forever. The hard part is money: I'm engaged to Mark, he's a plumber's apprentice, the wedding's next summer, and I've got about two weeks' wages saved after paying the deposit on the church hall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, people round here never trusted it anyway. Our customers want to talk to a person, especially the funeral families. I'd say that after church on Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, AI was never my main worry. Dennis is sixty-three and talks about retiring. If Dennis (her boss) retires and shuts the shop, there isn't another design job in this town, and Mark (her fiancé) and I aren't moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and do the work properly. I'd ask Dennis straight out what his plans are, so I'm not caught short. Mark and I would trim the wedding a bit, maybe a buffet instead of a sit-down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not about computers. About Dennis and the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Dennis did retire, have you thought about taking the business on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've thought about it, but I'd need money I haven't got, and I'm not good enough yet to run it alone. Maybe if Dennis stayed on two days a week to teach me. My dad might help a little, he's a farm manager, but they're not rich.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any routine work the small tools would touch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dennis might start using something for the football fixtures posters, they're the same every week. That's my Monday morning gone, but I'd not cry about it.

say: I'd say **people round here** never trusted AI anyway.
I'd say customers, especially **funeral families**, want a person.
think: My real worry is **Dennis retiring** and closing the shop.
There's **nowhere else** in town for a junior designer.
do: Keep doing the work **properly** for local customers.
Ask Dennis **straight out** about his retirement plans.
Switch the wedding to a **buffet** to save money.
feel: **Worried**, but about Dennis and the **wedding**, not computers.
S0.quote: If Dennis (her boss) retires and shuts the shop, there isn't another design job in this town, and Mark (her fiancé) and I aren't moving.
fieldNote: Her pressures are **local and personal**: an ageing boss and a wedding bill.
She values **family and church** ties and won't leave town.
She'd consider **taking over** the shop with help.

steps.text: Ask Dennis (her boss) directly about his retirement plans
Switch the wedding meal from sit-down to a buffet
Cut back spending to rebuild savings after the hall deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, people will lose the personal touch. I'd say businesses should still choose to hire local people. I wouldn't blame the government, that's not their job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think Dennis would use it to keep going without me. He could do the newsletters and posters with a machine and keep the funeral work himself. A machine can do the parish newsletter for nothing, so Dennis (her boss) won't need a junior to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Dennis if I could take on more of the face-to-face work, the families and the football club. If he said no, I'd ask at my aunt's florist, because people still need flowers arranged by hand. I'd lean on Mark's wage and push the wedding back a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, really. I've never wanted to use these tools, and now they'd be the thing that decides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've never used the tools. Would you start now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't think I would, if I'm honest. It doesn't feel right for the funeral work, and I'd be poor at it anyway. I'd rather do something with my hands than learn something I don't believe in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you feel about pushing the wedding back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heartbroken, but sensible. My mum would say God's timing is better than ours. Mark would say whatever I want, which isn't helpful.

say: I'd say losing the **personal touch** is a shame.
I'd say businesses should still **choose local** people, without the government stepping in.
think: Dennis could keep going **without me** using a machine.
Only the **funeral work** would stay with a person.
do: Ask Dennis for more **face-to-face** work with families and the club.
Ask at **my aunt's florist** if he says no.
Push the **wedding back** a year and lean on Mark's wage.
feel: **Alarmed** that tools I won't use would **decide my future**.
S1.quote: A machine can do the parish newsletter for nothing, so Dennis (her boss) won't need a junior to do it.
fieldNote: She refuses the tools on **feel and principle**, choosing **hands-on** work.
She **doesn't blame government**, but expects businesses to choose people.
**Postponing the wedding** is her biggest sacrifice.

steps.text: Ask Dennis for the funeral and football club work
Ask her aunt about a job at the florist
Push the wedding back a year
Live mainly on Mark's apprentice wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't know what to say. I'd probably say we need to pray about it, and look after each other. I'd not go on about it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd have nothing. Everything at the shop is design on a screen, and in two years nobody needs that. Mark's plumbing would last till 2031 when the robots come, but he's only an apprentice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't really know. I'd go to my aunt's florist and beg for hours. We'd cancel the church hall and get married at the registry office. Maybe we'd move in with my parents on the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked. I'd have no idea what to do and no money to work it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd beg for hours at the florist. Is that a plan or a hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Working at my aunt's florist is a hope, not a plan, and I'd know that even while I asked her. I'd be leaning on my family and the church, and that's not a plan either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mark?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll be fine, because that's what you say. I'd not believe it. I think I'd cry in the van.

say: I'd say we need to **pray** and look after each other.
I'd **stay quiet online** and talk to people at church.
think: All my design work is on a screen, so it's **useless by 2028**.
Mark's **plumbing** work lasts only until robots arrive in 2031.
do: Ask my aunt's **florist** for any hours.
Swap the church hall for a **registry office** wedding.
Move in with my **parents on the farm**.
feel: **Panicked**, with no idea and **no money** to work it out.
S2.quote: Working at my aunt's florist is a hope, not a plan, and I'd know that even while I asked her.
fieldNote: She has **no plan** and no money, and says so honestly.
Her support network is **family and church**, not the state.
She'd **downsize the wedding** to a registry office.

steps.text: Ask her aunt for any hours at the florist
Swap the church hall booking for a registry office wedding

Lean on her family and church friends for help

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so people should get practical. Learn a trade, look after your family. I'd say that at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, Dennis would probably carry on another couple of years, then retire right as it hits. Five years would let me learn floristry properly. Mark would be qualified by then, and plumbing has a few years after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my aunt to teach me floristry on Saturdays from next year. We'd keep the wedding date but cut it down. I'd stay with Dennis as long as he'd have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed still, but with something to do. Better than the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why floristry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Funeral flowers are like funeral booklets, because you're helping a family through the worst week of their life. And my aunt's got the shop, so it's family, not a stranger taking a chance on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens after 2034, when robots can do hands-on work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, and I'd rather not think too far. I'd hope people still want flowers from a person for weddings and funerals. That's the same kind of thing I love about the booklets.

say: I'd say people should **get practical** over the next few years.
I'd tell people at church to **learn a trade** and look after family.
think: Dennis would likely keep going, then **retire as AGI hits**.
Five years lets me **learn floristry** properly before robots arrive in 2034.
do: Learn **floristry** from my aunt on Saturdays from next year.
Keep the **wedding date** but cut it down.
Stay with **Dennis** as long as he'll have me.
feel: Still **alarmed**, but having **something to do** helps.
S3.quote: Funeral flowers are like funeral booklets, because you're helping a family through the worst week of their life.
fieldNote: She connects her **new trade** to what she loves about her current one.
Family provides the **training route**: her aunt's shop.
She still expects to **lose design work**, hence alarmed.

steps.text: Learn floristry at her aunt's shop on Saturdays from next year
Keep the wedding date but cut guests and costs
Stay at Dennis's shop as long as the work lasts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning, so nobody has an excuse. Families and churches should help people make the switch. I'd say that to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'd stay in design for a few years, then move to the florist properly. Dennis will have retired by then anyway. We'd have time to have children and for Mark to set up on his own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay with Dennis and learn all I can. In about three years, I'd start at my aunt's florist part-time. We'd go ahead with the wedding as planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a bit, but I can see the path. Ten years is a long time in a small town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said children. Would AI change your plans there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In that world Mark (her fiancé) and I would still have children, but I'd want our money settled before AI takes my design work. It would only mean waiting until the florist hours were settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Dennis's shop? Would you ever take it over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not in this picture. There's no point taking over a design shop that has ten years left. I'd rather put any money into Mark's van and tools.

I'd say **families and churches** should help people switch.
think: I'd stay in design a few years, then **move to floristry**.
We'd have time for **children** and for Mark's own business.
do: Stay with Dennis and **learn all I can**.
Start **part-time** at my aunt's florist in about three years.
Go ahead with the **wedding as planned**.
feel: A bit **anxious**, but I can **see the path**.
S4.quote: In that world Mark (her fiancé) and I would still have children, but I'd want our money settled before AI takes my design work.
fieldNote: Ten years gives her a **calm path**, but her design job still ends.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. I'd have nothing and no idea. What would help is apprenticeships for grown-ups, proper ones with a wage, and businesses choosing to keep local people. Not handouts, just a fair chance to learn something real.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe the funeral families. When a grieving family hands me a shoebox of photos, they want a person who'll take care with them, not a machine.

headlineQuote: When a grieving family hands me a shoebox of photos, they want a person who'll take care with them, not a machine.
portrait: Chloe is a **27-year-old junior** designer at a three-person shop on Church Lane.
She **never uses AI** and cares most about the funeral booklets she makes.
She's engaged to a **plumber's apprentice**, with a wedding next summer and two weeks' savings.
She leans on **family and church**, and wants work and apprenticeships, not handouts.
Her fallback is **floristry** at her aunt's shop, and fast AGI leaves her panicked.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd have **nothing** to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **adult apprenticeships** and businesses that keep **local people**.
